docstring_ux_aitone_pass.description: A single _length_violation() helper is reused across append, extend, insert, pop, remove, clear, __delitem__, __iadd__, __imul__, frombytes, fromfile, and __setitem__. The resulting ValueError always reads "width-changing mutation is not allowed" without naming which call triggered it, so in a stack of chained operations the user cannot tell whether it was e.g. `+=` vs `.append` vs a resizing slice assignment without inspecting the traceback frame.
docstring_ux_aitone_pass.suggestion: Pass the operation name into the helper (def _length_violation(self, op): ...) and interpolate it, e.g. "append() would change the length ... FixedLengthBitVector length is invariant (N bits)".
docstring_ux_aitone_pass.verifyReason: Accurate as to the code: bytemaker/bitvector/fixed.py:33-38 defines a single `_length_violation()` helper reused verbatim by append/extend/insert/pop/remove/clear/__delitem__/__iadd__/__imul__/frombytes/fromfile/__setitem__ (lines 40-88), and the ValueError message never names the triggering operation. The quote matches exactly. So the finding is real, not fabricated, and the suggestion (thread an `op` name into the helper) is actionable. However it is a marginal low-value polish item and I downgrade confidence for two reasons the report underweights: (1) the existing message is already unusually informative for this codebase — it states the invariant, the current width, and the exact remedy ("make a resizable copy with BitVector(...) first"), well above the terse norm of sibling messages like "pop from empty BitVector" or "negative shift count" which also don't name operations; (2) the report's core premise — that "the user cannot tell whether it was `+=` vs `.append`" without extra effort — is weak, because each of these is a distinct method/statement whose name and source line appear in the top frame of the standard traceback that always accompanies the raised ValueError, so the operation identity is already surfaced for free. It's a fair, honest low/low suggestion but sits at the nitpick boundary rather than being clearly worth the maintainer's attention.

docstring_ux_aitone_pass.title: classproperty getter/setter/deleter AttributeErrors omit the attribute name
docstring_ux_aitone_pass.description: classproperty raises 'unreadable attribute', "can't set attribute", and "can't delete attribute" with no attribute name. Python's own built-in property was upgraded in 3.11 to include the attribute name (e.g. "property 'x' of 'C' object has no setter"). On a class with several classproperties, a bare "can't set attribute" forces the developer to hunt for which one they touched. Since __get__ already receives objtype, the class and attribute are available to name.
docstring_ux_aitone_pass.suggestion: Include context, e.g. raise AttributeError(f"unreadable classproperty on {objtype.__name__}") and f"can't set classproperty on {type(obj).__name__}", matching the informativeness of built-in property in 3.11+.
docstring_ux_aitone_pass.verifyReason:
The cited code is present verbatim in bytemaker/utils.py at lines 40 ("unreadable attribute"), 45 ("can't set attribute"), and 51 ("can't delete attribute"). The factual claims check out: classproperty is applied to multiple properties on a single class (e.g. ByteConvertibleString in bittypes/string.py defines codepoint_changes, _reverse_codepoint_changes, _codepoint_change_regex, _reverse_codepoint_change_regex), so a bare "can't set attribute" would not disambiguate; and Python 3.11 did upgrade the built-in property to name the attribute, which this backport predates. So the finding is accurate, not a fabrication, and correctly scoped as low severity.

However, it leans nitpick and its practical impact is largely hypothetical, so I downgrade confidence: (1) These three strings are the verbatim pre-3.11 CPython property messages — a faithful, conventional backport idiom rather than author sloppiness. (2) classproperty is an internal utility used ONLY as a read-only getter throughout the codebase; no .setter/.deleter is ever applied, so the __set__/__delete__ branches (lines 45/51) and the fget-is-None getter branch (line 40) are effectively unreachable in current usage. The "developer hunting for which classproperty they touched" scenario therefore rarely, if ever, materializes. It is a legitimate, actionable low-severity polish suggestion (name the class/attribute to match 3.11+ property), but marginal in real-world value. Accept as real, keep severity low, lower confidence to reflect the mostly-unreachable error paths.

docstring_ux_aitone_pass.title: Filler "only really be true" in __eq__ docstring

This will only really be true if both objects are BitVectors." docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.title: BoundField docstring recommends `f.bits & bv`, which raises TypeError (BoundBits defines no bitwise dunders)
docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.reason:
The finding's headline claim is factually wrong: `f.bits & bv` does NOT raise TypeError — it runs and returns the correct bit-plane result. I verified this empirically in bytemaker/structs.py against the current code:

    class S(Struct):
        x: UInt8
    s = S(x=0b10101010)
    f = s.sizedview.x
    bv = BitVector('11110000')
    f.bits & bv   # => BitVector('10100000')   (also | and ^ work)

The finding correctly observes that BoundBits (structs.py:1090) defines no `__and__`/`__or__`/etc. and that `__getattr__` (line 1141) is not consulted for implicit dunder dispatch — both true in isolation. But it stops there and never accounts for Python's reflected-operator fallback. Since `type(f.bits).__and__` is absent, Python evaluates `bv.__rand__(f.bits)` (bitvector_speedup.py:884), which does `bv & f.bits` -> `_binary_bitwise_op` (line 868) -> `BitVector(f.bits)`. That constructor (line 311) checks `getattr(source, "__Bits__", None)`, and because BoundBits.__getattr__ forwards `__Bits__` to the underlying live BitVector, the cast succeeds and the AND computes correctly ('10101010' & '11110000' = '10100000'). So the docstring at lines 898-899 presents a genuinely runnable, correct idiom.

The docstring is also careful to pair each plane with the right operand type: `f.value & m` (value plane, int mask) vs `f.bits & bv` (bit plane, BitVector). The only failing form is `f.bits & <plain int>` (int has no __rand__ accepting BoundBits), but the docstring never writes that — it writes `& bv`. There is at most a very minor latent fragility (the idiom relies on the RHS being a BitVector, and works via reflected dispatch rather than a defined dunder), but the docstring does not mislead and the claimed high-severity user-facing breakage does not exist. Rejecting as inaccurate.

docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.title: pack_tuple 'at every width' narrowing claim does not fully hold on the aligned tier
docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.reason: Rejected as a nitpick. The docstring (bytemaker/plans.py:241-242) reads: "Out-of-range integers narrow C-style (wrap) rather than raising, at every width." Its grammatical subject is already "integers" — it makes no claim about float or bytes fields. The finding's own reasoning concedes it is "largely accurate" and that "the claim is about integers specifically." The purported gap — that _wrap_values (line 264, "if spec is not None and isinstance(v, int)") passes float ("f") and bytes ("b") fields through unchanged — is irrelevant to a sentence that explicitly speaks only about integers. Crucially, for integers the guarantee actually DOES hold at every width: on the shiftmask tier "v &= mask" (line 255) always wraps, and on the struct tier struct.pack raising for an out-of-range int triggers _wrap_values, whose spec-not-None + isinstance-int condition is always true for integer fields (kinds "u"/"s" get a non-None spec at lines 153-163). I found no integer width where wrapping fails, so "at every width" is a true statement, not an overstatement. The suggested rewrite ("Out-of-range integer fields ... at every integer width") is nearly identical to the existing "Out-of-range integers ... at every width" and adds no real precision. This is new-July narrative-style code with no REF counterpart, so it is not a tone/drift issue either. Not worth maintainer attention.

docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.title: codepoint_changes Returns type omits the BitVector-mapping input it accepts
docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.reason: The finding's factual claims are all accurate against current code (bytemaker/bittypes/string.py:105-140): the docstring at line 108 does say "Set this with a str->str mapping or a BitVector -> BitVector mapping", the Returns at 114-115 declares only Optional[HashableMapping[str, str]], and the getter body at 124-134 does decode BitVector keys/values to str via cls.decoding(k) before returning. The docstring is field-list style consistent with this reference-era file's norm, so this is NOT a case of flagging the intentional narrative style. However, this is a nitpick, not a real docstring defect. The docstring is not broken by any of the flag-worthy criteria: no wrong/missing/renamed param, no stale ref, no example that misruns, and crucially the Returns does NOT lie -- it correctly states str->str, which is exactly what the getter returns. A setter that accepts two input forms and a getter that returns one normalized form legitimately have different type statements; describing "set with X or Y" and "returns Z" is coherent and not misleading. The finding itself concedes it is "Not misleading enough to be a behavior bug." The requested fix is a single optional clarifying clause -- pure subjective preference. This does not rise to the level of a real inconsistency worth the maintainer's attention.

docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.title: Frozen aggregate impl labeled '0.12' in _legacy_aggregate.py but '0.11/0.12' in aggregate_types.py for the same snapshot
docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.reason:
The quoted text is present: bytemaker/_legacy_aggregate.py:2 says "The frozen 0.12 aggregate-conversion implementation." and bytemaker/conversions/aggregate_types.py uses "0.11/0.12" at lines 5 and 81. But the claimed inconsistency does not hold up on a close read, so this is a nitpick that isn't worth the maintainer's attention.

The wrapper does NOT uniformly label the frozen snapshot "0.11/0.12". At aggregate_types.py:15 it says "One deliberate behavior fix vs 0.12" -- pinning the frozen baseline the code forked from at 0.12, exactly matching _legacy_aggregate.py:2's "frozen 0.12". The two "0.11/0.12" uses are contextually about spanning two releases, not tagging the freeze point: line 5 "Public API is unchanged from bytemaker 0.11/0.12" is an API-stability claim across a release span, and line 81 "the per-call cost of the 0.11/0.12 aggregate functions" describes a cost characteristic that held across both versions. So "0.12" (freeze point) vs "0.11/0.12" (release span over which API/cost were stable) is a defensible distinction, not mechanical drift describing "the identical frozen snapshot with different labels."

The finding's own description concedes it is "imprecise rather than provably wrong" and rates it low/low, and I could not verify the "verbatim copy of ref commit 1a894a2 = v0.11.0" premise because the ref tree at the given path contains no readable .py source (only empty subdirs / __pycache__), so the assertion that the freeze version is provably 0.11.0 is unsubstantiated here. There is no demonstrated error to fix, only a preference for a uniform version string, and the prose is internally coherent when read in context. This is a subjective low-value observation, not an actionable documentation defect.

docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.title: Numeric array element type error omits the field name and array type
docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.reason:
The finding's live repro is accurate but its core claim — that the array element branch is inconsistent because it "omits the field name and array type" — is factually wrong. I reproduced both stores: `s.x = 'a'` (scalar UInt8 field) and `s.xs = ['a','b','c']` (UInt8*3 array) each raise the IDENTICAL bare `TypeError: 'str' object cannot be interpreted as an integer`, with no field name in either case. The directly analogous sibling path is the scalar numeric field descriptor `_UIntField.__set__`/`_SIntField.__set__` (structs.py:171, 192), which also calls bare `operator.index(value)` and produces the same nameless error. The docstring at structs.py:1403-1407 explicitly states the array coercion is done "*exactly* as the scalar field descriptors do," and it is. So `Array._coerce_one` (structs.py:1416-1424) is CONSISTENT with the established Struct convention for numeric stores, not worse.

The finding contrasts against the struct-element branch (1409-1414), but that branch handles a by-reference StructMeta element via `isinstance` — it has no `operator.index` analog, so its named message is not a relevant comparison for the numeric case. The report mischaracterizes a library-wide property (all numeric Struct stores raise bare TypeErrors from `operator.index`) as an array-specific inconsistency. Worse, applying the suggested fix only to the array branch would CREATE the inconsistency it claims to remove: `s.xs=['a']` would name the field/type while `s.x='a'` still would not.

There is a real but different and much smaller observation buried here: numeric Struct field stores generally give unhelpful bare type errors. That is a low-severity, whole-Struct UX rough edge (not array-specific) and is the intended C-integer-promotion `operator.index` store path. As reported — medium/high, framed as an array-branch inconsistency — it is inaccurate and unfair, so I reject it.

docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.title: The field-naming validator (validate_tuple) is off by default and never reached via the bulk path
docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.reason:
The finding's literal facts check out (plans.py:292-311 validate_tuple builds field-named messages like `f"{f.name}={v!r} outside [{lo}, {hi}]"`; structs.py:133 `DEBUG_VALIDATE = bool(os.environ.get("BYTEMAKER_DEBUG"))` defaults False; structs.py:838-839 gates the call under `if DEBUG_VALIDATE:`; pack_tuple at plans.py:238-259 never calls it). But the framing that drives its severity is wrong, so it is not a fair/actionable finding.

1. Its central claim -- "the one method that could tell a user precisely what is wrong is effectively hidden" / "the good error path is dormant" -- is false. A field-named diagnostic already exists independently of validate_tuple: the field descriptors _UIntField/_SIntField call `_warn_narrowing(iv, v, f"field {self._slot.__name__[4:]!r}")` at store time (structs.py:174,197 -> bittype.py:51-56), naming the field. validate_tuple is redundant with that and is explicitly documented as a MIGRATION-time re-check ("re-validate every field range at pack time during migrations," structs.py:43-44), used for values that bypass the descriptors.

2. It frames silent wrap as swallowing errors, but silent C-style narrowing is the documented, uniform library contract: pack_tuple's own docstring (plans.py:239-242) says "Out-of-range integers narrow C-style (wrap) rather than raising, at every width," and NarrowingConfig (bittype.py:44) says "Default off (silent C semantics)." This is the library's stated C-analogous thesis, not a defect.

3. Its premise that users only get a context-free struct.error ignores that stores narrow at set time (structs.py:19 example `d.x = 0x10005 -> 5`), so out-of-range values normally never reach pack. Two documented opt-in knobs cover the diagnostics need (BYTEMAKER_DEBUG -> validate; BYTEMAKER_WARN_NARROWING -> warn).

No doc lies, no broken behavior, no user-facing breakage. The suggestion (advertise validate_tuple / call it in pack_tuple) is a minor opinion that argues against the intended silent-C default. Subjective API-ergonomics rooted in a mischaracterization of deliberate design -- does not clear the fair/accurate/actionable bar.

docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.title: Lazy uN/sN factory accepts absurd/unsupported widths with no validation, failing late and cryptically
docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.reason: Inaccurate. I reproduced the behavior and the finding's core claims do not hold. (1) "Any integer width works" is documented, intentional design, not a footgun — bytemaker/fields.py:8 states "Any integer width works, not just the pre-declared ones." I confirmed empirically that byte-aligned absurd widths round-trip perfectly end-to-end: `class Big(Struct): x: u80000` instantiates, packs to 10000 bytes, and parses back correctly; paired `u1000` fields (250 bytes) also round-trip. There is no bug and no cryptic failure for valid (byte-total) widths. (2) The claim that bad widths "fail late and cryptically, deep inside the plan compiler or during pack/parse, as an opaque error far from the annotation site" is false. A non-byte-aligned total fails at CLASS-DEFINITION time (StructMeta.__new__ -> compile_plan, plans.py:461-466), before any instantiate/pack/parse, with a clear, contextual message: "Big: total size is 99999 bits, not a whole number of bytes; pair or pad sub-byte fields until the total is a multiple of 8" — it names the owner, the exact bit count, and the remedy. That is early and actionable, the opposite of the described symptom. (3) The suggested fix (add an upper width sanity bound) contradicts the module's stated purpose (C-struct-like arbitrary-width fields); a 1000-bit field is legitimate. The only true kernel — that fields.py:83/102-111 and int.specialize() do no upper-bound check — is intentional and causes none of the claimed user-facing pain, so it does not warrant a medium/high report.

docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.title: 'Unsupported format' errors in to_pyint/to_bitstring don't list the valid formats
docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.reason: The two lines are quoted accurately: bytemaker/bittypes/int.py:138 `raise ValueError(f"Unsupported format: {bin_format}")` (to_pyint) and :302 `raise ValueError(f"Unsupported format: {rep_format}")` (to_bitstring), and neither enumerates the accepted set nor uses repr on the value. But this is a nitpick that doesn't warrant maintainer attention. (1) Both format params are typed Literal["twos_complement","signed_magnitude","ones_complement"], so a type-hint-following caller cannot reach the near-miss scenario the finding dramatizes; the near-miss spellings ('2s','sign_mag') are speculative. (2) It is pre-existing legacy code, not new July churn — the exact message text 'Unsupported format:' is present in the 4-week-old reference int.cpython-311.pyc, so it is neither a regression nor tied to the high-churn Struct/plans/fields code the audit prioritizes. (3) The proposed repr+enumeration convention is NOT already established in this file: the sibling `TypeError(f"Unsupported type: {type(self)}")` at line 103 and the range-error messages at lines 223/240-243/252-255 all use the same terse `f"...: {value}"` form, so this flags no inconsistency — it proposes a new convention. The message is not misleading; it correctly names the problem and echoes the offending value. A legitimate low-value polish suggestion, but below the bar for a reported finding given the audit's steer toward new, high-value issues and away from nitpicks.

docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.title: FixedLengthBitVector.pop advertises index/default parameters it never honors
docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.reason: Rejected. The finding's core premise is factually wrong. It argues "pop on a fixed-width vector could legitimately just read (it does not need to shrink if it returned without deleting)." But pop is by contract a remove-and-return operation: the base impl at bytemaker/bitvector/bitvector_native.py:1162 does `del self._bits[index]`. A non-deleting pop would violate the list-like/MutableSequence contract every backend implements. So the claim that users "will reasonably expect it to work" rests on a misreading of pop's semantics — a fixed-width vector MUST refuse pop precisely because pop mutates length. Not a discoverability trap: (1) the override keeping the full base signature `(self, index=None, default=None)` is the deliberate, consistent pattern in this file — insert(self, index, value) and remove(self, value) at fixed.py:46,52 likewise preserve their full base signatures and unconditionally raise; singling out pop is arbitrary. (2) The finding's own remedy is already implemented: the error message (fixed.py:34-38) says "length is invariant (N bits): width-changing mutation is not allowed on a FixedLengthBitVector; make a resizable copy with BitVector(...) first", and the class docstring (fixed.py:22-24) explicitly lists `pop` among the methods that raise ValueError. The suggested "note that pop is unavailable... point to an alternative" is thus already satisfied. This is a subjective nitpick built on an incorrect model of pop, with a non-existent remedy gap.

docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.title: Public deep-import path: BitVector only reachable via bytemaker.bitvector, not a metaphor-free top-level export
docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.reason: Both core premises are factually false. (1) The finding's title says BitVector/FixedLengthBitVector are "only reachable via bytemaker.bitvector, not a top-level export," but bytemaker/__init__.py re-exports all four names: imports at lines 49-54 and __all__ entries at lines 74-77 (BitVector, FixedLengthBitVector, BitsCastable, BitsConstructible). `from bytemaker import FixedLengthBitVector` works, so users are NOT forced down a nested path. The suggestion's action item ("confirm re-exported from top-level bytemaker") is already satisfied. (2) The "footgun" claim mischaracterizes the layout: FixedLengthBitVector is defined in bitvector/fixed.py (line 17), NOT in bitvector.py. bitvector.py is not a "facade" over fixed.py; it is a sibling module that defines only BitVector/BitsCastable/BitsConstructible, so it correctly omits FixedLengthBitVector from its __all__ (advertising a symbol it doesn't define would be wrong). The actual facade is the package __init__.py, which correctly imports from both modules and exports all four. `from bytemaker.bitvector import FixedLengthBitVector` working is the intended design, not an accidental inconsistency. The only true observable (bitvector.py __all__ differs from the package __all__) is expected because they are different modules with different contents. No genuine discoverability problem exists.

docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.title: bin()/oct()/hex() separator applies to characters, not bytes, contradicting the parameter name and docs
docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.reason:
The finding is inaccurate for its primary cited location and overstated overall. It cites to01 (lines 564-578) and quotes `bits_per_sep = 8 * bytes_per_sep` as evidence of a "characters not bytes" bug — but that line is CORRECT: for binary, 1 byte = 8 chars, so grouping by `8 * bytes_per_sep` chars groups on exact byte boundaries. The docstring "chunks of `bytes_per_sep` bytes" is accurate for to01/bin, so the title's claim that the separator "applies to characters, not bytes, contradicting the parameter name and docs" is false at the location cited.

The only factually correct sub-claim is about the separate `tobase` path (lines 507-513/526-534): for base 32 and 64, `chars_per_byte = int(8/bits_per_char + 0.999999999)` ceils (5 and 6 bits/char both give 2 chars/"byte"), so `bytes_per_sep=1` groups every 12 bits for base 64, not 8 — verified computationally. But this is unavoidable: a 6-bits-per-char base cannot be split on byte boundaries without splitting characters, and the code already flags the incomplete base story with `# TODO support non-multiple-of-two bases`. For the byte-aligned bases (2, 8, 16) that users actually reach via bin/oct/hex, grouping is on clean boundaries.

The "users cannot get a nibble/hex-digit-level separator" point is a feature-request framing, not a doc-vs-behavior contradiction — the parameter is explicitly named `bytes_per_sep` and documented as bytes; nibble grouping was never promised. Net: the finding is built around a location where code and docs are correct, and its one accurate point is a minor, essentially-unavoidable edge case already acknowledged by a TODO. Not worth the maintainer's attention as framed.

docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.title: from_bytes_aggregate(is_array=True) silently accepts non-multiple lengths and yields a short final entry
docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.reason:
The finding's central claim is factually wrong. It asserts the is_array path "silently accepts non-multiple lengths and yields a short final entry, producing either a bogus decoded entry (from a too-short buffer)." I verified the code (bytemaker/conversions/aggregate_types.py:229-237) and ran it against a real byte-aligned dataclass: a non-multiple length does NOT silently yield anything. Every terminal decode path enforces a strict length check that raises before any bogus value is produced — plan.parse (plans.py:500-506), from_bytes_individual (_legacy_aggregate.py:204-209), and legacy from_bytes_aggregate (_legacy_aggregate.py:410-415). Concretely, from_bytes_aggregate(b'ABCDE', Rec, is_array=True) with a 2-byte entry raises "ValueError: Cannot convert b'E' to <class 'Rec'> because the number of bits in the bytes object (8) does not match the number of bits in the unit type (16)" — a loud, reasonably descriptive error that names actual vs expected bit counts, not the silent corruption the finding describes.

Two sub-facts the finding cites are individually true but misframed: the 7-byte-at-3 chunking does produce a short final slice [b'ABC', b'DEF', b'G'] (confirmed), and the zero-width case (empty dataclass) hits range(0,n,0) and raises "ValueError: range() arg 3 must not be zero" (confirmed, an opaque message). But the short-slice fact is harmless because the strict length check catches it downstream. Only the zero-width->opaque-range-error slice is a genuine defect, and it is a narrow edge case (decoding an empty/zero-width dataclass as an array) yielding one confusing message — a low-severity polish nit, not the medium-severity silent-mis-decode described.

Because the headline and primary evidence materially misrepresent the actual behavior (claiming silent bogus output where the code in fact fails loudly), the finding as written fails the accuracy bar and should be rejected. Note the same chunking logic exists in the frozen oracle (_legacy_aggregate.py:430-446), so this is not new-code regression either. The suggested multiple-of validation would slightly improve the message wording, but the current behavior is not misleading in the way claimed.

docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.title: Width-alias lazy resolver gives no hint that zero/negative widths are invalid
docstring_ux_aitone_rejected.reason:
The mechanism is accurately described: the resolver at bytemaker/__init__.py:135-147 uses `re.compile(r"(u|s)([1-9][0-9]*)")`, so `u0`/`s0` do not match and fall through to `raise AttributeError(f"module {__name__!r} has no attribute {name!r}")` (the same is true in bytemaker/fields.py:83-91). But this is not a real, actionable audit finding.

1. `u0`/`s0` are genuinely invalid names — a zero-width integer field is meaningless — so the standard "module 'bytemaker' has no attribute 'u0'" is the correct, expected Python attribute-lookup message, not a misleading one. This is not a broken behavior, a lying Returns/Raises, or a stale doc.

2. The docstring claim "uN/sN field aliases exist for any width" (bytemaker/__init__.py:18-20) is not falsified by `u0` failing, because 0 is not a width. The reference-voice module docstring is fine; nothing here mixes styles or drifts in tone.

3. The core argument — that a user makes exactly the `u0` off-by-one typo AND concludes the whole lazy-alias feature is broken — is speculative. Countless non-matching names (`u`, `x8`, `uint8`) also fall through generically, which is correct.

4. The proposed fix is a speculative UX nicety (special-case an error hint for a name the library correctly rejects), and the suggested message text is itself somewhat AI-flavored. For a sole-user library where backward-compat/polish is weighted near zero, this is exactly the kind of low-value enhancement to skip. It reads as a feature request dressed as a defect, not an evidence-backed documentation/consistency/tone problem. Rejecting as a subjective nitpick.
